title: DOAH 26-0053 Recommended Order: KALIYAH LANIER vs. LOADING...GASTROBRUNCH
text:
STATE OF FLORIDA
DIVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
KALIYAH LANIER,
Petitioner,
vs. Case No. 26-0053
MJ2 LLC D/B/A
LOADING...GASTROBRUNCH,
Respondent.
/
RECOMMENDED ORDER
Pursuant to notice, a final hearing was conducted on May 5, 2026, via
Zoom teleconference, before Linzie F. Bogan, a duly-designated
Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) of the Division of Administrative Hearings
(DOAH).
APPEARANCES
For Petitioner: Kaliyah Sharnell Lanier, pro se
5020 West Irlo Bronson Memorial Highway
Kissimmee, Florida 34746
For Respondent: No one appeared
STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES
Whether Respondent, MJ2 LLC d/b/a Loading…Gastrobrunch
(Respondent or MJ2), subjected Petitioner to discrimination on the basis of
her race in violation of section 760.10, Florida Statutes, and whether
Respondent retaliated against Petitioner for the exercise of protected rights
under section 760.10.1
1 All references to the Florida Statutes are to the 2025 version unless otherwise noted.

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
On May 30, 2025, Petitioner, Kaliyah Lanier (Petitioner), filed with the
Florida Commission on Human Relations (FCHR) a Complaint of
Employment Discrimination alleging that Respondent discriminated against
her based on her race and color, and retaliated against her for the exercise of
protected rights. FCHR investigated the allegations. On November 25, 2025,
FCHR issued a written determination that there was no reasonable cause to
believe that an unlawful practice occurred.
On or about December 21, 2025, Petitioner timely filed a Petition for
Relief with FCHR. On January 6, 2026, FCHR referred the case to DOAH for
the assignment of an ALJ so that a final hearing could be held. The final
hearing was convened on March 5, 2026. Petitioner appeared for the final
hearing but no one appeared on behalf of Respondent.
On March 5, 2026, an Order Regarding Proper Respondent was entered,
in part, because information provided by FCHR to DOAH did not properly
identify Respondent. Per the Order, Respondent’s three managers and its
registered agent were provided with notice regarding this matter and the
style of the case was updated to reflect the proper Respondent. The case was
continued, sue sponte, and the final hearing was rescheduled for May 5, 2026.
As noted in the Order Regarding Proper Respondent, Jahnae Allen is
listed as a “manager” for Respondent with the Florida Department of State.
Notice of the final hearing scheduled for May 5, 2026, was mailed to
Ms. Allen at the address on file with the Department of State, and the same
was returned to DOAH as undeliverable and the envelope containing the
notice was marked as “vacant” by the United States Postal Service (USPS).
None of the other notices mailed on March 31, 2026, to Respondent’s
2

registered agent and two other managers regarding the rescheduled hearing
were returned to DOAH by USPS.
Petitioner testified on her own behalf and called no other witnesses.
Petitioner’s two Exhibits were admitted into evidence. Neither party filed a
transcript of the final hearing nor submitted a proposed recommended order.
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. From February 14, 2025, until May 11, 2025, Petitioner worked for
Respondent as a table busser. Petitioner’s job responsibilities included
clearing and resetting dining room tables, assisting servers, maintaining the
cleanliness of the dining room, and other related functions. According to
Petitioner, she normally worked about 25 hours per week for Respondent,
earned $12.00 per hour, and averaged about $50.00 per week in tips.
2. In April 2025, Respondent “drastically reduced” Petitioner’s work hours
and scheduled her to work “only one shift for the entire” month. Although the
exact date is unclear, Petitioner, at some point, complained to Jahnae Allen,
one of the managers at the restaurant, about her reduced work hours during
April and that she had not been scheduled to work any hours during May.
Respondent did not respond to Petitioner’s complaint.
3. Although Respondent did not schedule Petitioner to work in May,
Respondent contacted Petitioner on May 10, 2025, and offered her a double
shift. Petitioner reported to work, as agreed, and during her shift one of the
managers yelled at Petitioner and accused her of giving free food to
customers. According to Petitioner’s undisputed and credible testimony, a co-
worker “immediately corrected [the manager] and explained that customers
had moved tables on their own and that [Petitioner] had done nothing
wrong.”
4. At 4:11 a.m. on May 11, 2025, Petitioner was included on a group chat
message in which the manager informed Petitioner that her employment was
3

terminated due to reasons related to her work “performance.” Petitioner’s
undisputed and credible testimony was that before the termination of her
employment she had never received any “warnings, write-ups, coaching, or
documentation indicating performance concerns.”
5. Petitioner contends that she was “discriminated and retaliated against
based on [her] darker complexion and for asking about [her] reduced hours to
no hours.” In explaining her allegations, Petitioner testified that her white
co-workers were treated more favorably by Respondent and in support
thereof offered the following examples.
6. First, Petitioner contends that she was disciplined more severely than
her white co-workers. According to Petitioner, a white co-worker named Joy
“seated customers at the Viking table despite being instructed not to use that
table.” Petitioner’s undisputed and credible testimony was that despite the
warning, Joy “was not publicly reprimanded, yelled at, or addressed in the
group chat.”
7. Second, Petitioner contends that she was excluded from membership in
the “OG” workgroup. This group consisted of white individuals who were
apparently original employees of the restaurant. According to Petitioner, the
use of the term “OG” “felt racially charged rather than accidental.”
8. Finally, Petitioner, in support of her claim, testified that “[o]ther
employees openly stated in the group chat that they were running late [for
work], [and] no public reprimand” was issued to them by Respondent.
Petitioner did not present evidence that she was disciplined for reporting late
to work while her white co-workers were not.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
9. DOAH has jurisdiction of the subject matter of and the parties to this
proceeding. §§ 120.569, 120.57(1), and 760.11(7), Fla. Stat.
4

10. The Florida Civil Rights Act of 1992 (Florida Civil Rights Act or the
FCRA), chapter 760, prohibits discrimination in the workplace. The FCRA is
modeled after Title VII of the Civil Rights Acts of 1964 and 1991, 42 U.S.C.
§ 2000, et seq. (Title VII), so that federal case law regarding Title VII is
applicable to construe the FCRA. See Castleberry v. Edward M. Chadbourne,
Inc., 810 So. 2d 1028, 1030 (Fla. 1st DCA 2002).
11. Section 760.10 states the following:
(1) It is an unlawful employment practice for an
employer:
(a) To discharge or to fail or refuse to hire any
individual, or otherwise to discriminate against any
individual with respect to compensation, terms,
conditions, or privileges of employment, because of
such individual's race, color, religion, sex, national
origin, age, handicap, or marital status.
* * *
(7) It is an unlawful employment practice for an
employer, an employment agency, a joint labor
management committee, or a labor organization to
discriminate against any person because that person
has opposed any practice which is an unlawful
employment practice under this section, or because
that person has made a charge, testified, assisted, or
participated in any manner in an investigation,
proceeding, or hearing under this section.
12. Respondent does not dispute that it is an “employer” as defined in
section 760.02(7), which provides the following:
“Employer” means any person employing 15 or more
employees for each working day in each of 20 or more
calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar
year, and any agent of such a person.
13. Florida courts have determined that federal case law applies to claims
arising under the Florida Civil Rights Act, and as such, the United States
Supreme Court’s model for employment discrimination cases set forth in
5

McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973), applies to claims
arising under section 760.10, absent direct evidence of discrimination. See
Harper v. Blockbuster Ent. Corp., 139 F.3d 1385, 1387 (11th Cir. 1998);
Paraohao v. Bankers Club, Inc., 225 F. Supp. 2d 1353, 1361 (S.D. Fla. 2002);
Fla. State Univ. v. Sondel, 685 So. 2d 923, 925 n.1 (Fla. 1st DCA 1996); Fla.
Dep’t of Cmty. Aff. v. Bryant, 586 So. 2d 1205 (Fla. 1st DCA 1991).
14. “Direct evidence is ‘evidence, which if believed, proves existence of fact
in issue without inference or presumption.’” Rollins v. TechSouth, Inc., 833
F.2d 1525, 1528 n.6 (11th Cir. 1987) (quoting Black’s Law Dictionary 413 (5th
ed. 1979)). In Carter v. City of Miami, 870 F.2d 578, 582 (11th Cir. 1989), the
court stated:
This Court has held that not every comment
concerning a person's age presents direct evidence of
discrimination. [Young v. Gen. Foods Corp., 840 F.2d
825, 829 (11th Cir. 1988)]. The Young Court made
clear that remarks merely referring to
characteristics associated with increasing age, or
facially neutral comments from which a plaintiff has
inferred discriminatory intent, are not directly
probative of discrimination. Id. Rather, courts have
found only the most blatant remarks, whose intent
could be nothing other than to discriminate on the
basis of age, to constitute direct evidence of
discrimination.
15. Petitioner offered no evidence that would satisfy the stringent
standard of direct evidence of discrimination.
16. Under the McDonnell analysis, in employment discrimination cases,
Petitioner has the burden of establishing, by a preponderance of evidence, a
prima facie case of unlawful discrimination. If the prima facie case is
established, the burden shifts to the employer to rebut this preliminary
showing by producing evidence that the adverse action was taken for some
legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason. If the employer rebuts the prima facie
case, the burden shifts back to Petitioner to show by a preponderance of the
6

evidence that the employer’s offered reasons for its adverse employment
decision were pretextual. See Tex. Dep’t of Cmty. Aff. v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248
(1981).
17. To prove a prima facie case of unlawful employment discrimination
under chapter 760, Petitioner must establish that: (1) she is a member of the
protected group; (2) she was subject to adverse employment action; (3)
Respondent treated similarly situated employees outside of her protected
classifications more favorably; and (4) Petitioner was qualified to do the job
and was performing her job at a level that met the employer’s legitimate
expectations. See, e.g., Jiles v. United Parcel Serv., Inc., 360 Fed. Appx. 61, 64
(11th Cir. 2010); Burke-Fowler v. Orange Cnty., 447 F.3d 1319, 1323 (11th
Cir. 2006); Knight v. Baptist Hosp. of Miami, Inc., 330 F.3d 1313, 1316 (11th
Cir. 2003); Williams v. Vitro Servs. Corp., 144 F.3d 1438, 1441 (11th Cir.
1998); McKenzie v. EAP Mgmt. Corp., 40 F. Supp. 2d 1369, 1374-75 (S.D. Fla.
1999).
18. Petitioner has not established a prima facie case of unlawful
employment discrimination.
19. The undisputed evidence demonstrated Petitioner is an African-
American female and is therefore a member of a protected group.
20. The undisputed evidence demonstrated Petitioner was fired from her
position with MJ2 and was therefore subject to an adverse employment
action.
21. Petitioner was qualified to hold the “busser” position at MJ2, and
Petitioner’s undisputed evidence is that she was performing her job at a level
at or above expectations.
22. As to the question of disparate treatment, the applicable standard was
recently revised in Lewis v. City of Union City, Georgia, 918 F.3d 1213, 1218
(11th Cir. 2019): “[A] plaintiff asserting an intentional-discrimination claim
under McDonnell-Douglas must demonstrate that she and her proffered
comparators were ‘similarly situated in all material aspects.’”
7

23. State courts in Florida have found that a person suffers “disparate
treatment” in his or her employment, in violation of Title VII—and, by
extension, the FCRA—when he or she is singled out and treated less
favorably on the basis of his or her status as a member of a protected class
than other employees who are otherwise similarly situated in all relevant
respects. Johnson v. Great Expressions Dental Ctrs. of Fla., P.A., 132 So. 3d
1174, 1176 (Fla. 3d DCA 2014); Valenzuela v. Globeground N. Am., LLC, 18
So. 3d 17, 23 (Fla. 3d DCA 2009).
24. Petitioner offered no evidence as to the disparate treatment of
similarly situated employees outside of her protected classification.
Specifically, Petitioner did not present evidence that similarly situated white
employees were not also terminated by group chat, or that white individuals
remained employed at MJ2 despite being accused of giving free food to
customers.
25. While it is undisputed that her work hours were reduced during April
and May, Petitioner presented no evidence that the work hours of similarly
situated white bussers remained unchanged during this period.
26. Discriminatory intent may be proved by inference, but a trier of fact
“cannot infer discrimination from thin air.” Lizardo v. Denny’s, Inc., 270 F.3d
94, 104 (2d Cir. 2001), citing Norton v. Sam’s Club, 145 F.3d 114, 119 (2d
Cir.1998). Mere speculation or self-serving belief on the part of a complainant
concerning motives of a respondent is insufficient, standing alone, to
establish a prima facie case of intentional discrimination. See Lizardo, 270
F.3d at 104 (“Plaintiffs have done little more than cite to their mistreatment
and ask the court to conclude that it must have been related to their race.
This is not sufficient.”). See also Norton, 145 F.3d at 120 (anti-discrimination
law “does not make employers liable for doing stupid or even wicked things; it
makes them liable for discriminating….”). (emphasis added).
27. While Petitioner may have experienced less than desirable treatment
while employed at MJ2, the evidence is insufficient to reasonably infer that
8

any perceived or actual difference in treatment was as a result of illegal,
discriminatory animus. Petitioner failed to prove disparate treatment based
on her race.
28. As to Petitioner’s retaliation claim, the court in Blizzard v. Appliance
Direct, Inc., 16 So. 3d 922, 926 (Fla. 5th DCA 2009), described the elements of
such a claim as follows:
To establish a prima facie case of retaliation under
section 760.10(7), a plaintiff must demonstrate:
(1) that he or she engaged in statutorily protected
activity; (2) that he or she suffered adverse
employment action; and (3) that the adverse
employment action was causally related to the
protected activity. See Harper v. Blockbuster Entm’t
Corp., 139 F.3d 1385, 1388 (11th Cir.), cert. denied
525 U.S. 1000, 119 S. Ct. 509, 142 L.Ed.2d 422
(1998). Once the plaintiff makes a prima facie
showing, the burden shifts and the defendant must
articulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for
the adverse employment action. Wells v. Colorado
Dep't of Transp., 325 F.3d 1205, 1212 (10th Cir.
2003). The plaintiff must then respond by
demonstrating that defendant's asserted reasons for
the adverse action are pretextual. Id.
29. Petitioner made no evidentiary showing that any employment or
postemployment action by Respondent was causally related to any statutorily
protected activity she took while an employee. Petitioner’s retaliation claim
derives from her contention that MJ2 terminated her employment after she
complained about her reduced work hours. Perhaps a reduction in work hours
could support a retaliation claim, see, e.g., Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission v. White and Sons Enterprises, 881 F.2d 1006 (11th Cir. 1989),
but such is not the case herein. Petitioner’s complaint about reduced work
hours, without connecting or otherwise tethering her concern to how the work
hours of similarly situated white employees remained uncut, merely reduces
her complaint to nothing more than an employee grievance that fails to rise
to the level of being statutorily protected activity. In other words, Petitioner
9

did not engage in statutorily protected activity when she complained to
Respondent about a reduction of her work hours, and she, therefore, failed to
meet her burden with respect to her claim of unlawful retaliation.
30. In conclusion, Petitioner failed to present a prima facie case of
discrimination based on race or color, and failed to show that her dismissal
from employment by Respondent was in retaliation for her exercise of
protected activity.
RECOMMENDATION
Based on the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, it is
RECOMMENDED that the Florida Commission on Human Relations issue a
final order finding that MJ2 LLC d/b/a Loading…Gastrobrunch did not
commit an unlawful employment practice, and dismissing the Petition for
Relief filed in this case.
DONE AND ENTERED this 4th day of June, 2026, in Tallahassee, Leon
County, Florida.
